doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Monk Rowe praises the unison lick on Night in Tunisia
summary: Rowe recalls hearing the band at the Iridium; Hampton says the lick copied a Charlie Parker break and that he adjusts difficulty to the players.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we are in West Orange, New Jersey for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Slide Hampton with me today. And you know an interviewer is not supposed to tell stories, but I must tell you that a couple of years ago I heard your band at the Iridium.

And I happened to get a seat that was right at the end of the saxophone section. And I was able actually to see the music. And I saw this passage coming up. I said this is totally impossible. They cannot play this. And not only did they play it but the whole band, in unison, played this lick that I was just astounded at.
Yes. I could not believe they pulled it off. You write some challenging music.
When we first played that and Paquito D’Rivera heard that he said, “God, what was that?”
It was a unison lick, right?
Yeah. I actually made it up — it was actually a sort of a copy from the Charlie Parker break that he had made.
Yeah. That was great. I just had to tell you that, that it certainly made an impression.

Well we just played that arrangement — not that arrangement, another arrangement of “Night in Tunisia” when I was in Holland a couple of weeks ago. And when I got ready to give them that break too but I didn’t have the courage to give it.
Really. So you do have some sympathy for where you are at and who is playing the music?

Oh yeah. You have to adjust you know. Because if you find a real enthusiastic bunch of guys then you give them any difficult music. And they’re glad to have the challenge. Other guys, “Oh man, this is difficult,” you know.
